key_insight: The paper turns long documents into reusable "memory atoms" instead of one oversized adapter, enabling a model to compile and compose smaller pieces of context on demand. This makes document-level reasoning more flexible, efficient, and query-specific.
problem_solved: It addresses the high memory and latency cost of long-context inference in LLMs, and the limitations of prior context-distillation methods that compress an entire document into a single monolithic adapter.
method: Convert document context into compact memory atoms that capture reusable pieces of information.
Learn to compile these atoms into lightweight adapters for a given query or task, rather than generating one fixed adapter per document.
Compose multiple atoms as needed so the model can retrieve and combine relevant knowledge more selectively.
impact: For practitioners, this offers a faster and more memory-efficient way to use long documents with LLMs. It can improve scalability and query-specific performance in document understanding, multi-step reasoning, and other long-context applications.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: document input -> memory atoms -> compiled adapter -> query answer
Comparison graphic: single monolithic adapter vs. composable memory atoms
Memory/time chart showing reduced inference cost versus long-context attention
Icon set for document, atom blocks, adapter, and lightning bolt for efficiency
paper_title: Doc-to-Atom: Learning to Compile and Compose Memory Atoms
paper_authors: Xingjian Diao, Wenbo Li, Yashas Malur Saidutta, Avinash Amballa, Lazar Valkov
